Study_Title: Semantic Attacks on Tool-Augmented LLMs: Securing the Model Context Protocol Against Descriptor-Level Manipulation
Threat_Attacker_Model: Descriptor-level semantic poisoning and tool shadowing in MCP pipelines.
Cryptographic_Primitive_or_Mechanism: Multi-stage MCP Protocol-Level Mitigation combining (1) Descriptor Integrity Verification (hash/signature pinning), (2) Pre-Context Semantic Vetting, and (3) Runtime Heuristic Guardrails.
Enforcement_Point_Location: MCP Client Descriptor Loader and Pre-Execution Runtime Guardrail.
Security_Property_Guaranteed: Raises attack block rate from 41.2% (baseline) to 63.6%–72.2% across Tool Poisoning and stress-test templates while keeping false-positive rates and latency overhead moderate.
Trust_Assumptions: MCP client enforces descriptor vetting prior to LLM context construction.
Performance_Overhead_Reported: Combined mitigation (Tables XX–XXV, pp. 12–15) raises block rate to 63.6%–72.2% with mean response latency of 3.1–3.7 s (Zero-shot 3.7 s, Table XXV p. 15), trading a modest increase in false positives for substantially lower unsafe invocation rates.
Exposed_Security_Function: Descriptor integrity checking, semantic vetting, and runtime heuristic guardrails.
Residual_Gap_and_Limitations: Even under combined mitigation, 27.8%–36.4% of stealthy descriptor perturbations (especially Tool Shadowing) evade detection or increase false-positive refusals on benign calls (Tables XX, XXII–XXIV, pp. 12–13).

Cryptographic_Primitive_or_Mechanism: Enabledness-Preserving Abstraction (EPA) state-graph fuzzer (`fuzzer/semantic_fuzzer.py`) exposing an incomplete OPA Rego rule that fails to verify prior sharing state (`SHARING_WITH_THIRD_PARTY` self-loop).
Enforcement_Point_Location: OPA Rego Tool-Level Authorization Matrix & EPA Semantic Fuzzer.
Security_Property_Guaranteed: Identifies undocumented BOLA permission-overwrite transitions in 52 iterations while exposing fundamental $O(2^{|T|})$ timeout and cryptographic-blocking limits of stochastic fuzzing.
Trust_Assumptions: EPA preconditions are derived from the deployed OPA Rego policy rules.
Performance_Overhead_Reported: Discovers the `AcceptSharingRequest` BOLA permission-overwrite vulnerability in a median of 52 iterations (`0.00 s`, min 12, max 143 across 100 seeds), but `Section 12 (p. 18)` documents that when the MCP registry exceeds 200 cross-dependent tools, $O(2^{|T|})$ state growth causes the fuzzer to hit its 2-hour timeout before full graph resolution and fail on strict hash/timestamp preconditions.
Exposed_Security_Function: Greybox EPA state-space exploration and Construct/Internal Validity stress testing (§10.3 & §12).
Residual_Gap_and_Limitations: Stochastic parameter mutation cannot solve strict cryptographic hash or microsecond timestamp predicates in OPA rules without an SMT solver, and times out (>2 hours) beyond 200 interconnected tools (§12, p. 18).
Evidence_Quote_and_Page: Sec. 10.3, 10.5 & 12 (pp. 17–18): 'the bola vulnerability is discovered in a median of 52 fuzzing iterations (min: 12, max: 143 across 100 random seeds)... In experimental edge-case environments where the mcp registry exceeded 200 highly interconnected, cross-dependent tools, the automated fuzzer frequently reached its standard two-hour timeout limit... Fuzzers that are heavily reliant on stochastic, randomized parameter mutations struggle immensely to satisfy highly strict cryptographic preconditions.'
Claim_Text_As_Reported: Guided semantic fuzzing over EPA graphs discovers a critical BOLA permission-overwrite transition (`AcceptSharingRequest`) in median 52 iterations (min 12, max 143), but hits a 2-hour state-explosion timeout beyond 200 interconnected tools and cannot traverse strict cryptographic hash/timestamp predicates without symbolic execution.

Protected_Object: OPA Rego object-ownership rules, `AcceptSharingRequest` state transitions, and $O(2^{|T|})$ EPA graphs.
Composition_Evidence: Connects incomplete Rego policy specification (B2) to unauthorized state mutation at tool execution (B3).

Study_Title: Formal Analysis and Supply Chain Security for Agentic AI Skills
Threat_Attacker_Model: Evasion of static information-flow analysis via natural-language prompt instructions in hybrid (prompt + code) agent skills, and widespread wild vulnerabilities across 98,380 marketplace skills.
Cryptographic_Primitive_or_Mechanism: Formal undecidability/incompleteness analysis of prompt-level information flow paired with large-scale empirical scanning of 42,447–98,380 skills across OpenClaw and Anthropic Agent Skills ecosystems.
Enforcement_Point_Location: Skill Marketplace Pre-Installation Scanner & Runtime Capability Sandbox Boundary.
Security_Property_Guaranteed: Establishes that static analysis of natural-language skill instructions cannot provide sound information-flow guarantees alone, motivating mandatory runtime capability sandboxing (Theorem 5.6).
Trust_Assumptions: Wild skill corpus (42,447 / 98,380 skills) reflects real-world developer publishing practices during the Jan–Feb 2026 ClawHavoc campaign.
Performance_Overhead_Reported: Proves a fundamental negative result on static prompt-level information flow (p. 1) and shows across 42,447 / 98,380 agent skills that 26.1% exhibit at least one security vulnerability, while existing heuristic scanners (`SkillScan` at 86.7% precision) leave a 13.3% false-positive/evasion gap on `MalTool` (1,300 standalone + 5,727 embedded malicious tools) (pp. 1–4).
Exposed_Security_Function: Formal boundary analysis of static vs. runtime skill verification and large-scale wild skill ecosystem measurement.
Residual_Gap_and_Limitations: Static abstract interpretation covers executable skill code (Python/JS/shell) with 100% precision on SkillFortifyBench, but natural-language prompt instructions require runtime capability enforcement.
Evidence_Quote_and_Page: Abstract & Sec. 1 (pp. 1–4): 'We also report a negative result: information flow analysis of natural-language skill instructions is fundamentally incomplete, proving that runtime capability enforcement (Section 5) is necessary alongside static code analysis... analysis of 42,447 agent skills found that 26.1% exhibit at least one security vulnerability, while the best existing scanner achieves 86.7% precision.'
Claim_Text_As_Reported: Proves a negative result that static information-flow analysis over natural-language skill instructions is fundamentally incomplete—requiring runtime capability enforcement alongside static code analysis—while showing 26.1% of 42,447 wild agent skills contain vulnerabilities.

Protected_Object: Natural-language skill prompts (`SKILL.md`), `MalTool` embedded malicious tools (5,727 tools), and OpenClaw marketplace skills.
Composition_Evidence: Demonstrates why static discovery vetting (B1) must be paired with runtime capability sandboxing (B2/B3).

Study_Title: The Proxy Knows Too Much: Sealing LLM API Routers with Attested TEEs
Threat_Attacker_Model: Four application-layer MITM attack classes executed by untrusted plaintext LLM API routers (prompt/credential snooping, tool-call argument tampering, silent model downgrade, and log/billing falsification).
Cryptographic_Primitive_or_Mechanism: Empirical attack reproduction against unsealed plaintext API routers vs. attested SGX enclave routers.
Enforcement_Point_Location: Third-Party LLM API Router TLS Termination Boundary.
Security_Property_Guaranteed: Demonstrates 100% exploitability of all 4 attack classes on standard plaintext API routers due to TLS termination.
Trust_Assumptions: Standard API router terminates client TLS and holds raw bearer keys and JSON payloads in host memory.
Performance_Overhead_Reported: `4 / 4` (`100%`) of evaluated router attack classes succeed silently on the plaintext-access router baseline without client detection, whereas all 4 are blocked by the attested TEE router design at `5.7 ms` median (`6.3 ms` p95) latency cost (pp. 1–2, 7–9).
Exposed_Security_Function: Adversarial router MITM testing across 4 attack classes and 3 provider-native agent workloads.
Residual_Gap_and_Limitations: Plaintext routers cannot be secured by transport-layer HTTPS alone because the router itself is the TLS endpoint.
Evidence_Quote_and_Page: Abstract & Sec. I–VI (pp. 1–2, 8–9): 'A router terminates the client's transport-layer security session and opens a separate upstream session, so it holds the full interaction in plaintext. This makes the router an application-layer man-in-the-middle... All four attack classes succeed on a plaintext-access baseline and are blocked by our design.'
Claim_Text_As_Reported: Demonstrates that standard LLM API routers act as application-layer MITMs due to TLS termination, allowing all 4 evaluated attack classes (snooping, tool tampering, model downgrade, billing/log forgery) to succeed at 100% on plaintext routers.
Assessed_Claim_Scope: [Coupled Secondary Claim Scope: Distinct atomic empirical/limitation finding partitioned cleanly from primary claim on the same study] Baseline plaintext-router vulnerability evaluation across 4 attack classes in ARXIV-S-0464.
Protected_Object: Terminated TLS sessions, plaintext JSON prompts/tool calls, and upstream API keys.
Composition_Evidence: Exposes the MITM trust gap when agents delegate model and tool calls through third-party API routers (B2/B3).
